title: 100 AI People to Watch in 2027: The Engineers, Researchers and Founders Building What Comes Next
dek: The research, open infrastructure and business decisions behind AI’s next chapter. One documented contribution and one testable 2027 thesis for every person.

seo.title: 100 AI People to Watch in 2027: Engineers, Researchers and Founders
seo.description: 100 AI researchers, engineers, founders and innovators to watch in 2027, with their education, career history, dated funding figures and sources.

limitations: Public-record review of the retained claims and explicitly labelled editorial analysis; no interviews or audited company accounts.
Education dates and current jobs that could not be established remain unknown or explicitly attributed to dated records.
Company operating metrics are attributed claims. Private stakes and personal wealth are not estimated; pending transactions are not closed rounds.
This editorial selection is not a demographic survey, influence ranking or investment recommendation.

people.name: Alexander Wei
people.hook: Reasoning needs an auditable result
people.fact: Wei identifies his OpenAI research role and lists his participation in the CICERO team.
people.analysis: The business question concerns the gap between an impressive answer and an argument that can survive external checking. Reliable reasoning could reduce expensive expert review, but the review burden is part of the product economics.
people.watch: Publish reasoning results with inspectable artifacts and clearly attributable contributions.
people.risk: A benchmark improvement that does not transfer to useful, verifiable work.

profile.hook: [The Decoder's July 2025 report](https://the-decoder.com/openai-claims-a-breakthrough-in-llm-reasoning-on-complex-math-problems/) attributes to Alexander Wei's OpenAI team an experimental model scoring 35 of 42 points on the International Mathematical Olympiad, solving five of six problems. It describes a company-reported result, not an official medal awarded to the model.
profile.education: His [own research profile](https://www.alexwei.org/) records an A.B. and S.M. from Harvard in 2020 and a computer-science PhD from Berkeley in 2023, advised by Nika Haghtalab, Michael Jordan and Jacob Steinhardt.
profile.career: Wei won IOI gold in 2015 and a SODA 2019 Best Student Paper award. At Meta FAIR he co-authored CICERO, the Diplomacy-playing AI published in Science in 2022. He was at OpenAI by 2025 (start date not verified). On July 19, 2025, he and Noam Brown announced the IMO result, crediting general-purpose reinforcement learning and test-time compute scaling rather than task-specific methods.
profile.outlook: The July 2025 IMO result raises a harder question for Wei's team: can other mathematicians inspect and verify the reasoning?
profile.read: A strong competition result would weaken as evidence if it failed to transfer to independently verifiable mathematics.

people.name: Jerry Tworek
people.hook: The people behind reinforcement learning
people.fact: OpenAI credits Jerry Tworek with overall leadership within its reasoning-research section.
people.analysis: That is a more precise starting point than a talent-market headline. I want to understand whether the training approaches associated with reasoning systems become repeatable tools for useful work.
people.watch: Document a subsequent system or research artifact and its reliability outside a curated demonstration.
people.risk: Treating a historical leadership credit as proof of current employment or sole authorship.

profile.hook: Jerry Tworek's name appears beside overall reasoning leadership in OpenAI's o1 credits. After leaving OpenAI in January 2026, he launched Core Automation, shifting from a large lab to a startup focused on automating research.
profile.education: I could not establish his degree or graduation year from a primary education record.
profile.career: OpenAI's [o1 contribution record](https://openai.com/openai-o1-contributions/) names Tworek in overall reasoning leadership. [Business Today's January 7, 2026 report](https://www.businesstoday.in/amp/technology/news/story/openai-reasoning-chief-jerry-tworek-quits-after-7-years-heres-why-509827-2026-01-07) describes his departure after seven years and his work on Codex and post-training. [The Decoder's April launch report](https://the-decoder.com/ex-openai-researcher-jerry-tworek-launches-core-automation-to-build-the-most-automated-ai-lab-in-the-world/) describes a new lab pursuing learning algorithms beyond pretraining and reinforcement learning.
profile.outlook: [The Decoder reported in May 2026](https://the-decoder.com/ai-money-keeps-flowing-as-deepseek-plans-record-raise-and-core-automation-quadruples-valuation-in-weeks/) that Core Automation had raised $100 million at a $1 billion valuation and was targeting about $4 billion in another round. The latter was fundraising talk, not a confirmed closing. I am watching whether the lab turns that capital into repeatable improvements in model learning.

people.name: Jason Wei
people.hook: Making reasoning usable
people.fact: Wei says he works at Meta Superintelligence Labs and lists chain-of-thought and instruction-tuning work.
people.analysis: I am interested in the cost of turning a promising research technique into a dependable user experience. More reasoning is valuable only when the extra computation improves the result enough to justify its cost.
people.watch: Show reproducible improvements on tasks where quality and inference cost are both reported.
people.risk: A technique that improves a test score while making ordinary work slower or less dependable.

profile.hook: Jason Wei helped make chain-of-thought prompting a research result rather than a prompting anecdote; his current [personal site](https://www.jasonwei.net/) places him at Meta Superintelligence Labs after Google Brain and OpenAI.
profile.education: [Dartmouth's May 2023 alumni report](https://home.dartmouth.edu/news/2023/05/recent-alumnus-lectures-advances-ai) identifies him as a 2020 graduate. I do not infer an additional degree from his research appointments.
profile.career: His [CV](https://www.jasonwei.net/s/Jason_Wei___CV-f3xl.pdf) dates the Google Brain residency from October 2020 to December 2021, followed by research-engineer and research-scientist roles. He joined OpenAI in February 2023. The publication record includes FLAN, chain-of-thought prompting, emergent abilities, SimpleQA in 2024 and BrowseComp in 2025. The older CV still says OpenAI; his updated homepage is the source for the later Meta affiliation.
profile.outlook: Chain-of-thought research gives Jason Wei a specific 2027 challenge: show when a model's explanation reliably tracks how it reaches an answer. I would compare explanations against interventions, not just answer accuracy.
profile.read: A compelling reasoning benchmark would lose force if it rewarded persuasive explanations more than correct, reproducible answers.

people.name: Hongyu Ren
people.organization: Meta hiring report / OpenAI o1 record
people.hook: Attribution before the talent story
people.fact: Hongyu Ren appears among the foundational contributors to o1 reasoning research.
people.analysis: I would follow subsequent attributable research rather than use recruiting reports as a proxy for technical progress. The economic question is whether the work improves the cost or reliability of a reasoning system.
people.watch: Release a documented contribution that can be evaluated separately from employer prestige.
people.risk: Confusing participation in a large team with individual responsibility for every result.

profile.hook: Hongyu Ren appears among the foundational reasoning contributors in [OpenAI's o1 credit record](https://openai.com/openai-o1-contributions/). [Fortune reported in June 2025](https://fortune.com/2025/06/28/meta-four-openai-researchers-superintelligence-team-ai-talent-competition) that Meta hired him alongside three other OpenAI researchers.
profile.education: I could not retrieve a readable current primary education record during this review, so I do not publish the degree dates.

Fortune's June 28, 2025 report names Ren, Jiahui Yu, Shuchao Bi and Shengjia Zhao in the same hiring group. profile.read: For Hongyu Ren, I would look for evidence against this risk: confusing participation in a large team with individual responsibility for every result.

people.name: Sholto Douglas
people.role: Research discussed in a first-person interview
people.hook: Where the reward signal comes from
people.fact: Sholto Douglas discusses reinforcement learning and the difficulty of specifying useful rewards outside games.
people.analysis: I am watching that design problem because businesses need agents rewarded for finishing the right task, not merely producing persuasive output. A cheap automated reward that misses the real objective can create expensive errors.
people.watch: Demonstrate generalization to new tasks with transparent success criteria.
people.risk: Reward hacking or narrow training success presented as broad competence.

profile.education: A [University of Sydney report from August 2019](https://www.sydney.edu.au/engineering/news-and-events/news/2019/08/01/one-student-s-vision-to-build-an-automated-future.html) describes engineering honors studies, with a space-engineering major, alongside commerce. The [May 2025 Dwarkesh interview](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/sholto-trenton-2) describes his work scaling reinforcement learning at Anthropic. I use those first-person records for the move and research focus, rather than assigning him sole credit for Claude's capabilities.
profile.outlook: Douglas's May 2025 interview leaves dated predictions to compare with actual reinforcement-learning results in 2027. Next year those dated calls get graded in public.
profile.read: Anthropic / reinforcement learning's challenge is to avoid reward hacking or narrow training success presented as broad competence.

people.name: Joshua (Josh) Batson
people.hook: A model’s explanation is not its mechanism
people.fact: The contribution section credits Joshua Batson with leading the overall circuits project and helping develop its methodology.
people.analysis: This is a useful documentary distinction: a model’s fluent explanation is not evidence of how it reached an answer. I am watching whether mechanistic analysis becomes practical enough to help diagnose failures before deployment.
people.watch: Show interventions that identify and reduce specific failure modes across more than one model.
people.risk: An attractive visualization that does not reliably predict behavior.
detail: The record is unusually helpful about individual responsibility. Its contribution section separates project leadership, graph computation, interventions and visualization. I would preserve that attribution rather than describe one researcher as the person who explained an entire model.

My commercial question is whether an explanation changes a decision. If a method identifies a failure but cannot predict when it will recur or help prevent it, its value remains narrower than a buyer might assume. The next step is a reproducible intervention, not a more elaborate diagram.

profile.hook: Josh Batson helped turn Claude's internal computations into experiments that people can inspect; Anthropic's March 2025 circuit-tracing study examines rhyme planning, factual recall and the limits of a model's own account of its reasoning.
profile.education: [Gates Cambridge](https://gatescambridge.org/biography/6120) documents Yale mathematics studies and his move to Cambridge's Part III course. The Mathematics Genealogy record dates his MIT mathematics PhD to 2014, with Peter Ozsvath advising his work on knots and links.
profile.career: His mathematics record traces a move from knot theory into AI interpretability. Anthropic's [On the Biology of a Large Language Model](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/biology.html) credits him as a core contributor and correspondence author on the March 2025 attribution-graph project. Graph construction, interventions and visualization are distinct responsibilities; that credit does not mean one researcher explained an entire model. His Anthropic start date remains unestablished.
profile.outlook: Anthropic's circuit-tracing experiments give Batson's work a practical next test: can the explanations guide interventions that consistently change model behavior?
profile.read: Joshua (Josh) Batson's case depends on avoiding the opposite outcome:  explanations remain descriptive without predicting or preventing failures on new inputs.

people.name: Julian Schrittwieser
people.role: Contributor describing the project’s published work
people.hook: Reasoning that a checker can inspect
people.fact: Schrittwieser describes the AlphaProof system and links its published mathematical-reasoning paper.
people.analysis: Formal checking offers a clearer success condition than a convincing paragraph. I am watching whether that discipline spreads to useful software or scientific reasoning, while keeping formal benchmarks separate from commercial readiness.
people.watch: Make more results and their checking procedure accessible to outside researchers.
people.risk: Success confined to problems already shaped for a formal system.

profile.hook: Julian Schrittwieser's research path runs from Go-playing systems to formal mathematics. His own AlphaProof account ties the project to work at Google DeepMind from early 2022 to July 2024.
profile.education: I could not verify his degrees.
profile.career: [MIT Technology Review's profile](https://www.technologyreview.com/innovator/julian-schrittwieser/) describes his engineering work on AlphaGo and AlphaGo Zero. His [November 2025 AlphaProof account](https://www.julian.ac/index.html) says the system discovered Lean proofs for the 2024 International Mathematical Olympiad at silver-medal performance, with a paper published in Nature. It explicitly dates the work to his earlier Google DeepMind tenure. I retain that chronology rather than treating a later publication date as proof of a current employer.
profile.outlook: AlphaProof's formal-mathematics work makes independently checkable proofs the result I want to see next from Schrittwieser's research. I am watching whether reinforcement learning transfers from tightly specified games and formal proofs to tasks with ambiguous goals, incomplete feedback and a real cost when an agent makes a mistake.
profile.read: Julian Schrittwieser: the warning sign is success confined to problems already shaped for a formal system.

people.name: Neel Nanda
people.hook: Reverse-engineering the model
people.fact: Nanda says he leads DeepMind’s mechanistic interpretability team and identifies TransformerLens among his projects.
people.analysis: I see interpretability as an attempt to lower the cost of understanding failures that ordinary testing misses. The interesting business consequence would be better deployment decisions, rather than an explanation attached after something goes wrong.
people.watch: Produce reusable methods that help users locate actionable problems in deployed systems.
people.risk: Explanations that are informative to researchers but too fragile or costly for operational use.

profile.hook: Neel Nanda's [own biography](https://www.neelnanda.io/about) says he runs Google DeepMind's mechanistic interpretability team and mentors researchers through MATS. His route into that work began in pure mathematics and included quant-finance internships.
profile.education: His [own biography](https://www.neelnanda.io/about) says he studied pure mathematics at Cambridge and graduated in 2020, before a postgraduate year of AI safety internships; I do not infer an additional degree from that year.
profile.career: The same biography records internships at Jane Street and Jump Trading, followed by AI safety work at the Future of Humanity Institute, DeepMind and CHAI. He then did independent interpretability research and worked at Anthropic under Chris Olah before leading the Google DeepMind team. He describes the team's job as reverse engineering the algorithms and structures learned by neural networks; that is a concrete research mandate rather than a claim that every model behavior is already understood.
profile.outlook: Nanda's interpretability work at DeepMind needs to show which findings help researchers diagnose or change a model beyond a selected example. His mentoring work also makes the supply of trained researchers part of the story; a technique that only its original authors can operate has a limited auditing market.
profile.read: For Neel Nanda, I would look for evidence against this risk: explanations that are informative to researchers but too fragile or costly for operational use.

people.name: Jack Parker-Holder
people.hook: Training environments without building every world
people.fact: Parker-Holder describes work on world models and points to Genie as an example.
people.analysis: Synthetic environments could change the economics of training agents, but a convincing generated scene is not automatically a faithful simulator. I am watching the link between simulated experience and measurable performance elsewhere.
people.watch: Show that agents trained in generated environments improve on independent real-world tasks.
people.risk: Visual plausibility mistaken for physical accuracy or reliable transfer.

profile.hook: Jack Parker-Holder works on Genie, Google DeepMind's world-model research. [TechCrunch's August 2025 report](https://techcrunch.com/2025/08/05/deepmind-reveals-genie-3-a-world-model-that-could-be-the-key-to-reaching-agi) attributes 720p generation at 24 frames per second to Genie 3, then a research preview rather than a generally available product.

Then came Oxford and Google DeepMind's Open-Endedness team. His record includes PB2 (now in Ray Tune), ACCEL (ICML 2022) and AdA (ICML 2023 oral), then Genie (Feb 2024) and Genie 3, followed by Project Genie and a Street View integration announced at Google I/O. [His 2026 interview with Heise](https://heise.de/-11304842) discusses Street View integration and physical-world uses. The financial question is whether useful training scenarios can be produced more cheaply without sacrificing the accuracy needed for transfer to real environments.
profile.read: Google DeepMind's challenge is to avoid visual plausibility mistaken for physical accuracy or reliable transfer.

people.name: Lilian Weng
people.role: Research writer; reported OpenAI return, July 2026
people.hook: Separate self-improvement from the slogan
people.fact: Weng’s July 2026 notes discuss recursive self-improvement; her blog also examines test-time computation.
people.analysis: Her useful contribution is making the technical distinctions inspectable. I would separate better outputs, better training pipelines and a system modifying itself, because their evidence requirements and business implications are different.
people.watch: Explain a concrete feedback loop with measurable gains and its remaining constraints.
people.risk: A broad self-improvement claim with no clear baseline or independently checkable outcome.

profile.hook: Lilian Weng's [Lil'Log](https://lilianweng.github.io/) turns technical research into readable notes on reinforcement learning, hallucinations and model behavior. [July 2026 reporting](https://americanbazaaronline.com/2026/07/30/weng-leaves-thinking-machines-to-rejoin-openai-485496/) says she left Thinking Machines Lab and returned to OpenAI to work on recursive self-improvement.
profile.education: An [Ifanr profile](https://www.ifanr.com/1673220) reports Peking University studies beginning in 2005 and subsequent doctoral study at Indiana University Bloomington. I have not confirmed the degree award year from a university record.
profile.career: The July departure reporting describes earlier OpenAI robotics and safety work, followed by co-founding Thinking Machines Lab. I treat that as an attributed career account, not a primary employment register. Her own blog dates its learning notes to 2017 and provides a direct record of her writing. Research on reward hacking, hallucinations and test-time compute connects her public explanations to practical questions about model reliability.
profile.outlook: Weng's reported return to OpenAI shifts my attention to the artifacts that emerge from recursive self-improvement research. Faster research cycles would matter economically, but a claim of self-improvement needs a clear account of what was automated, what humans contributed and whether the gains replicate outside the team's own evaluation.
profile.read: Weng would lose my confidence over a broad self-improvement claim with no clear baseline or independently checkable outcome.

people.name: Liam Fedus
people.hook: What a founding round needs to produce
people.fact: The investor names Liam Fedus as a co-founder and describes a $300M founding round dated September 30, 2025.
people.analysis: I would judge the scientific bet by reproducible experiments and the cost of obtaining useful results. Capital provides room to attempt the work; it does not establish that an AI scientist or a profitable laboratory already exists.
people.watch: Produce independently inspectable experimental results and explain the laboratory loop.
people.risk: Large financing without evidence of useful scientific throughput.
detail: The investor's round amount is documented; a company valuation is not stated in that opened record. I would resist filling the gap by treating a fundraising discussion as a completed financing. The dated capital ledger separates what was announced from what a secondary headline might imply.

The cost of scientific progress includes equipment, experiments, repeat attempts and expert interpretation. That makes the financial test different from a software demonstration: I want to know whether useful experimental throughput improves, and which parts of the loop still require people.

profile.hook: Liam Fedus moved from language-model research to a company trying to automate scientific experiments. [Andreessen Horowitz's September 2025 announcement](https://a16z.com/announcement/investing-in-periodic-labs/) describes Periodic Labs as a combination of AI models and physical laboratories.
profile.education: His degree award dates remain unconfirmed in the primary university records available for this profile. A precise graduation year would imply evidence the sources do not provide.
profile.career: [OpenAI's o1 credits](https://openai.com/openai-o1-contributions/) name Fedus in reasoning-research leadership. The [Periodic Labs founding announcement](https://a16z.com/announcement/investing-in-periodic-labs/) identifies the subsequent company and its plan to connect AI with physical experimentation. These records document two distinct stages: improving language-model systems, then building infrastructure that can generate experimental data instead of relying only on existing text. They do not establish the full chronology of earlier employment or a personal ownership percentage.
profile.outlook: Periodic Labs' combination of models and physical laboratories makes repeatable experimental results the milestone to follow in 2027. I am watching whether automated experimentation produces reproducible materials results. Later fundraising discussions are not a closed round, and company capital raised is not Fedus's personal wealth.
profile.read: Liam Fedus's case depends on avoiding the opposite outcome:  autonomous experiments fail to produce materials with independently demonstrated practical value.

people.name: Misha Laskin
people.hook: Announcing a model and delivering it are different events
people.fact: The October 5 announcement promised the model’s weights and supporting artifacts later that month.
people.analysis: My focus is the sequence from announcement to accessible artifacts to independent evaluation. A model’s economic usefulness depends on the cost of serving useful outputs, not simply the size of its parameter count.
people.watch: Release usable artifacts and establish reproducible performance and serving costs.
people.risk: Company-only comparisons or limited access that prevents outside testing.

The model announcement describes a planned weights release later in October; announcing an open-weight model and delivering the artifact are separate milestones.

people.name: Luo Fuli
people.hook: Efficiency is also an engineering problem
people.fact: Fuli Luo appears on the report’s author list for a model using a mixture-of-experts and hybrid-attention architecture.
people.analysis: The question for 2027 is whether the serving system captures the architecture’s intended savings under actual workloads. A theoretical reduction is useful only if engineering turns it into reliable, cheaper service.
people.watch: Report deployment-level cost and latency alongside quality on comparable tasks.
people.risk: Architectural efficiency claimed without measuring the full serving pipeline.

people.name: Yao Shunyu (Vinces Yao)
people.hook: Learning from feedback without retraining every time
people.fact: Shunyu Yao is a co-author of research that uses linguistic feedback and episodic memory to improve an agent’s subsequent attempts.
people.analysis: That raises a practical question about where improvement should happen: in the model weights, the surrounding software or the task history. I would compare those choices by reliability, maintenance effort and cost.

people.risk: An agent carrying forward a mistaken explanation as if it were verified experience.

people.name: Lin Junyang (Justin Lin)

people.risk: A changing employer or fundraising story substituting for evidence about the product.

people.name: Yang Zhilin
people.hook: Agentic models need workflow economics
people.fact: Zhilin Yang appears on the author list of the Kimi K2 report, which describes an agentic model and released checkpoints.
people.analysis: My focus is the cost of completing an entire workflow, including retries and tool use. A good benchmark result can be a starting point, but it does not establish a low cost per successfully completed business task.
people.watch: Provide reproducible task-level results with total serving and retry costs.
people.risk: A high headline score that masks expensive or unreliable execution.

An external test should identify the model version, context length and evaluation date, so a later release cannot silently inherit the performance claims of an earlier one.

people.name: Chelsea Finn
people.hook: The robot has to learn outside the demonstration
people.fact: Finn identifies her Stanford appointment, Physical Intelligence co-founding role and research on learning through robotic interaction.

introduction: The 100 people below aren't the ones you already know. They contributed research, maintain open-source projects, build companies or shape the rules around AI. I selected them for a documented contribution and a concrete question to follow into 2027, rather than for a follower count or a presumed personal fortune.

I start with records: university biographies, papers, company statements and funding announcements. I distinguish what each source establishes from what it suggests. Company valuations are separate from personal wealth, fundraising discussions from closed rounds, and historical research credits from current jobs. Education gaps remain explicit rather than being filled from promotional biographies.

The list has five sections: frontier researchers, infrastructure engineers, founders, applied AI by industry, and people in safety, policy, investing and media. Numbering follows section order. It is not a ranking, and the section counts describe this editorial selection rather than the demographics or importance of the industry.

patterns.title: Research careers can become financing stories.
patterns.text: Periodic Labs connects research careers with a documented $300 million founding round in September 2025. Factory's September 2026 announcement records $200 million raised at a $5 billion company valuation. These are company events; neither discloses a founder's private stake or personal wealth.

patterns.title: An open project and a company are different assets.
patterns.text: vLLM, SGLang and llama.cpp make the distinction visible. A repository can remain open while its maintainers build a paid business or join another organization. I follow what happens to access, licensing and governance alongside the financing, rather than treating a star count as revenue.

patterns.title: Growth figures need their denominators.
patterns.text: Fireworks reports annualized revenue run rate, Modal reports a run rate and growth since September, and Mercor's gross contractor billings need separating from revenue it retains. I compare a figure only after identifying its date, definition and source; these are not interchangeable measures of commercial success.

patterns.title: A technical record survives a changing job title.
patterns.text: Papers, code releases and institutional biographies let me follow researchers across labs without assigning every later employer claim the same confidence. Tri Dao's updated Princeton title differs from his older CV; Jason Wei's homepage names a later affiliation than his CV. The dates and provenance matter.

patterns.title: Physical results are a different test from software benchmarks.
patterns.text: Robotics, materials and drug-discovery entries need evidence beyond a model leaderboard. A robot must work in unfamiliar surroundings, a proposed material must be made and tested, and a designed molecule must survive development. Financing pays for those attempts; it does not prove their outcomes.

faq.answer: This editorial selection includes Alexander Wei's mathematics-reasoning work, Jerry Tworek's move from OpenAI to Core Automation, Jason Wei's chain-of-thought research, Neel Nanda's interpretability work and Luo Fuli's MiMo contributions. Entries 1 to 21 cover the frontier section; the list is not a universal ranking.

faq.question: Who are the most important AI engineers right now?
faq.answer: The infrastructure section includes Woosuk Kwon's vLLM work, Ying Sheng's SGLang work, Georgi Gerganov's llama.cpp, Tri Dao's FlashAttention and David Soria Parra's MCP maintenance. Each has a specific code or research contribution to examine. See entries 22 to 41.

faq.question: Which AI founders are growing fastest?
faq.answer: I do not rank growth across incompatible measures. The entries include dated financing and operating records for businesses such as Lovable, ElevenLabs, Modal and Fireworks. ARR, annualized revenue, gross billings and company valuations measure different things.

faq.question: Why aren't Sam Altman, Dario Amodei or Demis Hassabis on the list?
faq.answer: This is an editorial selection of contributors and builders with specific work to follow. Better-known subjects also have separate profiles in the [Leaders index](https://visionarytalks.com/leaders/). A watchlist entry is not a substitute for a full financial biography.

faq.question: Do the valuations show what these people are worth?
faq.answer: No. A financing price, employee tender or acquisition consideration is a company or transaction measure. This watchlist does not estimate the individuals' personal wealth or undisclosed ownership stakes.

faq.question: How did you research this list?
faq.answer: I reviewed public research artifacts, university and company biographies, funding statements and attributed reporting. Unsupported details were removed or left unknown. The methodology below explains the scope; I did not conduct interviews or audit company accounts.

methodology.label: Selection
methodology.text: I chose people with a documented paper, codebase, product, company, policy contribution or investment record, and a concrete question to follow into 2027. Numbering follows section order.

methodology.label: Sources
methodology.text: I consulted university and lab pages, papers, company announcements and filings first. Reputable reporting fills some gaps. Source access failures and unresolved claims remain in the research audit.

methodology.label: Figures
methodology.text: A dated company valuation is separate from personal wealth. Company-reported revenue, funding announcements, employee tenders and acquisition consideration are different measures. Reported fundraising talks are not confirmed closed rounds.

methodology.label: Record distinctions
methodology.text: The ggml team joining Hugging Face does not disclose acquisition terms. Gamma's funding includes a secondary component, so funding-to-ARR is not a clean operating-efficiency ratio. Wix's Base44 consideration is not the founder's net worth. Reflection announcing Beam does not establish that promised weights have shipped.

methodology.label: Limits
methodology.text: I did not interview these people or audit their finances. Unknown education, graduation dates, current employment and private holdings stay unknown.

methodology.label: Corrections
methodology.text: If a record is outdated, use the [corrections page](https://visionarytalks.com/corrections/).
